state.misconception_label: Ignores negative sign when expanding bracket

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: John is expanding these three brackets: \( (x+5)(x-3)(x+6) \) He finds it helpful to split the first bracket and view the problem as follows: \( x(x-3)(x+6)+5(x-3)(x+6) \) He expands the brackets further. Before he simplifies, what are the terms than contain an \( \boldsymbol{x}^{2} \) ? I got \( \begin{array}{l}+6 x^{2} \\ +3 x^{2} \\ +5 x^{2}\end{array} \) because I forgot that two negatives multiply to a positive.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were expanding these brackets with everyday objects you can see and touch — would your method still give the right answer? Remember to consider the negative signs when multiplying.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, I'm not really sure what you mean by everyday objects, miss/sir? But I think I see what you're saying about the negatives... so when I expand 5(x-3), the minus sign matters, so it should be 5x minus 15, not 5x plus 15? Does that mean some of my x² terms should be negative?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were working with a pile of marbles — when you multiply a positive number by a negative number, the result is negative. So when you expand 5(x-3), it should be 5x - 15, not 5x + 15. This applies to the x² terms as well.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher repeatedly uses an unclear marble/objects metaphor that confuses the student, though the student does eventually recognize that negative signs matter in expansion, showing modest improvement despite rather than because of the scaffolding approach.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher attempts to use concrete analogies (everyday objects, marbles) but fails to meaningfully connect them to the algebraic structure of bracket expansion, resulting in superficial references rather than genuine experiential grounding.
